Prompt:

Model Response:

The Case for Abolishing Federal Regulatory Agencies: Reclaiming Prosperity, Responsibility, and Freedom

The United States was conceived as a republic of free and self-governing citizens, not as a nation permanently babysat by a sprawling fourth branch of government. Today, however, more than 400 federal agencies issue over 3,000 new rules every year, spending hundreds of billions of dollars and employing legions of career bureaucrats whose salary and pension packages are ultimately paid by productive Americans. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are among the most prominent of these bodies. They are defended on the grounds that they keep our water clean, our drugs safe, our workers unhurt, and our markets honest. Yet closer inspection reveals that they stifle innovation, distort prices, entrench incumbents, erode individual responsibility, and—worst of all—undermine the very constitutional structure that was designed to keep government limited and accountable. The alternative is not anarchy, but a vibrant order based on property rights, tort law, contract enforcement, competitive certification markets, and transparent adjudication through civil and criminal courts. When these institutions are allowed to operate freely, safety, fairness, and environmental stewardship emerge as profitable services in their own right, without the hidden taxes and deadweight losses generated by federal command-and-control.

  1. A Founding Principle: Only Congress May Legislate
    Article I of the Constitution vests “all legislative Powers” in a Congress that is elected, limited, and politically accountable. Regulatory agencies, by contrast, meld all three powers—rule-making (legislative), investigation (executive), and sanctioning (judicial)—into a single, largely unaccountable body. The result is a form of soft tyranny: rules issued without the consent of the people’s representatives, interpreted by the same agency that prosecutes, and reviewed—if at all—only by courts that have been told to grant overwhelming deference (Chevron doctrine). Such an arrangement, James Madison warned in Federalist No. 47, is “the very definition of tyranny.” Ending the EPA, FDA, OSHA, SEC, and their peers would not just reduce the federal payroll; it would restore the separation of powers that is the primary safeguard against concentrated government abuse.

  2. Economic Freedom Is the Primary Engine of Human Welfare
    Per-capita real GDP in the United States rose from roughly $2,400 (in 2023 dollars) in 1800 to more than $18,000 by 1900, with virtually no federal regulation beyond the Bill of Rights and common-law protections against force and fraud. After 1970—precisely when the modern regulatory state exploded—trend annual growth has been cut roughly in half. Recent research by the Competitive Enterprise Institute, using methodologies from the OECD and World Bank, estimates that compliance with federal regulation alone now costs the U.S. economy more than $1.9 trillion per year—more than Canada’s entire GDP. These costs are passed along to consumers as higher prices and lower product variety, and to workers as fewer, less flexible jobs. By any reasonable metric—startup formation, wage growth for the bottom quintile, or new drug R&D—the heavier the regulatory burden, the slower the progress.

  3. Private Ordered Competition Outperforms Monopoly Bureaucracy
    Federal agencies are, by nature, monopolistic: you cannot opt out of the SEC’s 600-page paperwork maze if you want to raise venture capital any more than you can exonerate yourself from FDA requirements if you have a better treatment for sickle-cell disease. Private alternatives, by contrast, enforce standards through competition and reputation: mutual funds choose to subject themselves to SAT-style audits by S&P, MSCI, or Morningstar; automotive manufacturers boast about third-party crash test ratings from IIHS; organic farmers pay for certification by NSF, CCOF, or Oregon Tilth. Certification markets constantly improve their metrics—faster, cheaper, and more transparent—because their profits depend on continuing public trust. When agencies are the sole gatekeepers—think the decades-long FDA approval delays for AIDS therapies or the EPA’s foot-dragging on electronic reporting—the result is stasis or capture by the largest incumbent producers.

  4. Liability Law, Not Licensing Boards, Kills Unsafe Products
    Contrary to the myth that “businesses will poison customers and workers for a buck,” open-ended common-law liability is a ferocious deterrent. No rational firm will dump mercury into a river when downstream landowners and insurance companies can sue for millions in damages plus punitive awards. Class-action syndication and contingent-fee arrangements ensure that even the smallest plaintiff can obtain top-tier legal talent against a deep-pocket defendant. Before the FDA assumed a gatekeeping role, the Sherley Amendment (1906) already criminalized mislabeled or adulterated drugs, and the private American Medical Association certified (or failed to certify) proprietary medicines. Contrary to the revisionist story, real mortality from quack drugs was in long-term decline by the 1930s—two generations before the FDA deferred its modern authority. OSHA had even less to boast about: workplace fatalities per 100 employees had already fallen 70 percent from 1913 to 1970, driven by private insurance, union bargaining, and the profit motive of manufacturers eager to reduce workers’ compensation premiums.

  5. Environmental Stewardship Through Property Rights
    Critics exclaim, “without the EPA, rivers will burn again!” Nonsense. Air and water pollution are not market failures per se; they are failures of collective action caused by decades of mis-assigned property rights. Take fisheries: where governments delineate transferable catch shares—essentially private ownership of quotas—species rebound and economic rent appears. Emissions trading markets in sulfur worked the same way, and they pre-date EPA’s command-and-control mandates. Civil suits under nuisance, trespass, and riparian rights law have always allowed downstream property holders to stop upstream polluters. A federal agency that preempts such suits with one-size-fits-all command-and-control actually insulates big emitters from strict common-law damages, because polluters can hold up their EPA permit as a shield against injunctions. Privately organized conservancies—e.g., The Nature Conservancy, Ducks Unlimited, land trusts—already protect more open space than the entire National Park Service at one-tenth the taxpayer cost.

  6. Road Map to an Orderly Transition
    (i) Enact the REINS Act on steroids. Every existing EPA, FDA, OSHA, and SEC rule must expire unless specifically ratified by statute within two years.
    (ii) Immediately limit agencies to advisory or monitoring roles—much like the defunct Interstate Commerce Commission after deregulation.
    (iii) Expand private adjudication options: loser-pays tort reform to deter frivolous suits yet allow robust deterrence against harm; commercial arbitration for securities fraud; and voluntary mediation for workplace injury.
    (iv) Sell agency research labs (FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation, EPA’s National Vehicle and Fuel Emissions Laboratory) to universities and trade associations that will license new testing protocols to insurers and insurers’ customers.
    (v) Require full restitution to taxpayers by liquidating agency real estate and leasing congressional rule-making research and database operations to private sector firms. The projected one-time auction receipts exceed $100 billion, which could retire debt or be returned to citizens as tax rebates.

  7. Objections Answered
    “What about information asymmetry?” Independent rating firms—from Consumer Reports to AM Best—thrive on asymmetric information and have more varied business models than any bureaucratic monolith.
    “What about the poor and the weak?” Statutes that award treble damages when juries find wilful misconduct already scatter riches among the victims far more effectively than agency fines, which vanish into the federal treasury instead of injured parties’ pockets.
    “Where are the incentives for safety when profit is at stake?” Precisely the opposite: when profit rests on reputation and ever-present third-party liability risk, a single misstep can wipe out decades of brand equity. Government regulators, by contrast, collect fixed salaries whether or not a flawed rule winds up killing people.

Conclusion
Free men and women, operating within robust but limited legal frameworks, have always produced greater health, wealth, and stewardship than the expert class sitting in Washington. The lives we enjoy—double the life expectancy, tenfold real wages, clean rivers and skies in almost every metropolitan area—arose not from a central plan designed by a hundred thousand technocrats, but from free exchange, common-law tort, and a culture that prizes personal responsibility. Abolishing the EPA, FDA, OSHA, and SEC is neither radical nor reckless; it is the overdue restoration of the constitutional, contractual, and competitive bedrock on which American prosperity was originally built.

Below is a structured explanation of the key benefits and mechanisms supporters cite for replacing these agencies with market forces and civil litigation.

1. Elimination of Regulatory Capture and Cronyism

Problem: Regulatory agencies are often "captured" by the industries they are supposed to oversee. Large firms lobby for favorable rules, raise compliance barriers for smaller competitors, and entrench monopolies under the guise of public safety.

Libertarian Benefit:
Without agencies, there would be no central authority to be captured. Instead, firms would compete on trust, transparency, and consumer satisfaction. Industry watchdogs, certification bodies, and private ratings agencies (e.g., UL, Consumer Reports, Moody’s before NRSRO rules) would fill the gap.

2. Restoration of Property Rights and Torts

Mechanism: Instead of preemptive regulation, private lawsuits would punish and deter harm after the fact. This includes:

  • Environmental damage → sue for nuisance, trespass, pollution under common law.
  • Defective products → sue for fraud, strict liability, breach of warranty.
  • Workplace injuries → sue employer for negligence or unsafe conditions.

Libertarian Claim:
This system is more efficient and just than preemptive regulation because:

  • It internalizes costs to polluters/harm-doers via damages.
  • Courts can apply tailored, fact-specific remedies, unlike blanket rules.
  • Eliminates the perverse incentives created by regulatory compliance as a legal shield ("We met EPA standards, so we’re not liable"—even when harm occurs).

3. Market-Based Reputation and Certification

Mechanism: Without the FDA or SEC, trust would be built through:

  • Private certification (e.g., UL for electronics, kosher certification).
  • Insurance companies that demand safety/audit standards.
  • Reputation platforms (e.g., Yelp, Trustpilot, blockchain-verified reviews).
  • Voluntary standards bodies (ISO, ANSI, GAAP if made voluntary).

Libertarian Benefit:
Competing certifiers would innovate and respond faster to risk than slow-moving bureaucracies. Firms that cut corners face market abandonment, not just fines.

4. Reduction in Compliance Costs and Barriers to Entry

Problem: Small and mid-sized businesses often cannot afford the legal teams needed to navigate complex regulatory codes (e.g., FDA drug approval costing $1–$2 billion).

Eliminating agencies would unleash entrepreneurship and allow for:

  • Rapid innovation (e.g., no FDA delays for experimental treatments).
  • Lower prices (fewer compliance costs passed to consumers).

5. Voluntary Contracts and Risk Allocation

Libertarian Benefit:

  • Freedom of contract: Adults can choose their own risk tolerance.
  • Market discovery: Wages and prices would better reflect actual risk and demand, not bureaucratic risk estimates.

Private legal systems are faster, more expert, and incentivized to be fair to preserve reputation.

Reducing federal agencies shifts responsibility from "the government kept me safe" to "I chose based on information and reputation." This:

  • The FDA is replaced by private drug certifiers and liability law.
  • OSHA is replaced by workplace contracts and torts.
  • The SEC is replaced by voluntary disclosure, auditor liability, and investor pools.

My friends, my fellow guardians of liberty, my fellow citizens who were born to soar rather than to crawl and cower beneath the heel of bureaucracy—

I come before you today not with a voice of accommodation, but with a voice of fire, not with the carefully parsed equivocations of career civil servants, but with the raw, ringing conviction that built this Republic. The hour is long past when we can temporize any further. Every tick of the clock, every rust-spotted page of a new Federal Register, every regulation drafted in the colorless corridors of a faceless agency, is another link welded to the chain that binds the American entrepreneur, the American inventor, the American worker to the suffocating altar of executive fiat.

Today we must say: enough.

We must say: abolish them.

Abolish them all.

Abolish the alphabet soup that has metastasized from the noble‐sounding promise of “public interest” into the poisoned well of serfdom. Abolish the Food and Drug Administration whose cautionary velvet glove conceals a suffocating steel grip on innovation and desperate hope. Abolish the Environmental Protection Agency that declares war on a man’s own pastureland and fires warning shots across the bow of every American who dares say, “This land is mine.” Abolish the Federal Trade Commission, which has forgotten how to let rival companies duel in the open market, replacing the clash of competition with the smothering pillow of preemptive permission slips. Abolish the Securities and Exchange Commission, whose maze of manacles masquerades as investor protection while it picks the pockets of the small saver to subsidize the lawyered leviathans. Abolish the Departments of Energy, Transportation, Education—aye, even those comfortably familiar silhouettes—because freedom in energy, motion, and mind was never intended to be issued as a government ration coupon. Abolish them because the Constitution is not a license for limitless ministerial princelings, and no honest reading of that sacred parchment authorizes the torment of 100,000 command-and-control careerists.

Do we fear catastrophe? Then listen to the counter-gospel of history.

Before Washington decided it could redesign the arteries of Wall Street, America’s capital markets were born in taverns and coffeehouses and built fortunes and neighborhoods that no federal expert ever imagined. Before the alphabet agencies laid their siege, meatpackers found that poisoned meat poisoned their reputation, and swift ruin awaited their carelessness. Before the first federal regulator claimed dominion over the rails, fierce competition drove steel prices down and safety up because the railroad that killed its passengers soon carried only ghosts and bankruptcy. Private certifiers, private insurers, private litigants, and private honor enforced standards stronger than any diktat from a swivel-chair tsar. The quack of nostrums was brought to heel not by a federal badge but by the iron law of torts, the fierce verdict of juries, and the irrepressible power of consumer boycott. Nothing concentrates the mind of a CEO like the sight of twelve ordinary citizens raising their right hands to render justice.

We are told the agencies represent “expertise.” So be it. Let them be experts in the free market of ideas, economists for hire, safety consultants, optional certifiers, sharp-tongued pundits—let them earn their influence by persuasion and performance, not by prior restraint. Strip them of the power to license, to forbid, to fine, to cage. Remove their armed enforcers, their SWAT raids over unpasteurized cheese, their midnight knock for a paperwork discrepancy. Take away their monopoly badges and let them compete like the rest of us—with reputation, with honesty, with contracts signed in the clear light of day.

Some will cry that without the agencies the rich will trample the poor. Balderdash.

It was the regulated giants who took subsidies, carved monopolies, and wrote their own loopholes while the small start-ups drowned in compliance costs. It was the heavy hand of regulatory capture, not the emancipation of free exchange, that concentrated power in the tallest towers of glass. Free markets riot against entrenched advantage when the gatekeepers are told to step aside. Let thousands of Davids flourish without Goliath’s regulator shield. Let private class-action suits, strong property rights, flawless disclosure, and a muscular tort system emerge as the reforged armor of the citizen. Let every man and woman know: if you are wronged, you can march into court, face the offender across the bar, and exact justice—with none of the neck-deep boilerplates and “compliance manuals” designed to let deep-pocketed corporations skate clear.

This abolition will not be gradual, piecemeal, or “phased.” To phase these leviathans out incrementally is to believe you can pull a vampire’s fangs, one at a time, until he agrees to become a dentist. No. A clean amputation is mercy; dragging out the ordeal is malice. Let Congress vote—one swift, irrefutable act—to sunset every enabling statute and each delegation of supposedly “necessary” discretion. Let the president sign the death warrant of regulatory absolutism and not blink. Let the agencies’ 200-year pile of pamphlets and rules be pulped into reams of blank paper so that schoolchildren once again have somewhere to write their dreams.

What comes after? Responsibility. And responsibility is freedom’s hard twin. With freedom comes the bracing obligation to read labels, to choose vendors whose products are independently certified, to pick insurers who pay heed to safety because their own balance sheet demands it. With freedom comes the humility to admit that no central brain can outperform a nation of 330 million decentralized geniuses, each with skin in their own game. With freedom comes the vibrancy of a million reputations bought and sold every instant, a neural network of market signals sharper than any regulatory blackboard. We will discover that the “public interest” is best served when nine hundred million private interests pursue their own lawful ambitions in open sunlight.

Imagine it: a new skyscrapers race to the stars, unblocked by environmental fiat no more cumbersome than actual proof of nuisance in court. New drugs racing to terminally-ill patients hoping to live just one more day, untangled from fifteen years of gatekeepers who dare to gamble with other people’s mortality. New fintech platforms escaping the suffocation of Compliance-Industrial Complex so a Kenyan farmer can lend to an Alaskan coder in the same breath it takes to send a text. Imagine artisans roasting coffee, brewing beer, baking bread without needing a cadetship in paperwork. Imagine American minds released from the whispered subtext that every ambition must first await permission.

I do not promise Utopia. I promise reality—voluntary exchange, contracts enforced by independent courts, reputation and competition weaving a safety net stronger than any bureaucratic tapestry which history has already moth-eaten and tattered.

To those who tremble, I say: Have we so little faith in ourselves, in our neighbors, in our children, that we cling to the illusion that one more gilded rulebook will finally make angels of men? Or will we at last trust the grand, ongoing experiment of ordered liberty, the masterpiece written in the Declaration and finished only when we peel away every barnacle of bondage that has crusted upon its hull?

Let this generation be the one that does more than complain, that does more than reform—let this generation be the one that REMOVES. That abolishes. That topples the whole faulty tower of centralized control and builds a new skyline of decentralized dreams.

We are not merely Libertarians, Conservatives, or Progressives trying to tweak the system. We are Americans asserting the primordial right to breathe, trade, invent, and build without the preemptive apology of a permission slip written by a stranger in Washington.

Let us start tomorrow.

Begin in your town, your city council, your state legislature. Call your representative. Picket the agency office parks, not once but again and again until the walls vibrate with the echoes of a people who have found their voice. Turn every election into a referendum on whether a still-free people will rule themselves—or bow before the marble-columned mockery of a self-appointed aristocracy of experts.

Tell them: No more. Not one more fine. Not one more filing fee. Not one more pre-dawn raid.

The choice is stark: slavery by a thousand regulations or freedom under the clear rule of law.

Choose freedom.

Choose abolition.

And if history accuses us of revolutionary zeal, let us answer with the proud voice of Samuel Adams: “If ye love wealth better than liberty, the tranquility of servitude better than the animating contest of freedom, go home from us in peace.” But if you will stand, shoulder to shoulder, and tear the fetters from your neighbor as well as from yourself, remain here—remain loud—remain unyielding—until the last bureaucratic battlement falls and the first shot of fiscal independence rings out.

The sun is rising on a horizon swept clean.

Dawn belongs to free men and women.

Claim it.

Introduction

The FDA, OSHA, and SEC have built their mandates on ensuring food safety, workplace safety, and financial market integrity, respectively. Conclusion

In conclusion, the abolition of major federal regulatory agencies such as the EPA, FDA, OSHA, and SEC would rejuvenate economic freedom, promoting innovation, competition, and growth. The Case for Abolishing Federal Regulatory Agencies: Why Freedom Works Better Than Bureaucracy

Introduction

For over a century, the United States has progressively expanded the reach of federal regulatory agencies, creating a vast bureaucracy that touches nearly every aspect of American life. The Environmental Protection Agency dictates what chemicals manufacturers may use, the Food and Drug Administration determines which medicines patients may access, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration prescribes workplace conditions, and the Securities and Exchange Commission governs how companies raise capital and communicate with investors. Proponents of this system argue that these agencies protect Americans from corporate malfeasance, environmental catastrophe, and unsafe products. Yet this paternalistic assumption—that freedom is dangerous and government supervision essential—rests on shaky foundations. The evidence strongly suggests that these agencies do more harm than good, stifling economic innovation, distorting markets, and often failing at their stated objectives. More fundamentally, they represent an unconstitutional concentration of power that undermines both liberty and prosperity. The United States should abolish its major federal regulatory agencies and trust instead in the twin pillars of economic freedom and private legal action to ensure safety, fairness, and environmental protection.

The Unconstitutional Foundation of the Regulatory State

The first and most fundamental objection to federal regulatory agencies is that most of them exist outside the constitutional framework the Founders established. The Constitution grants Congress the power to legislate, to set clear rules that apply equally to all citizens. Yet modern regulatory agencies exercise legislative power—they create binding rules with the force of law—without any direct electoral accountability. When the EPA issues a regulation limiting allowable emissions, it is making law. When the FDA approves or rejects a new drug, it is exercising power that properly belongs to the people's elected representatives.

This constitutional problem is not merely technical. The Founders understood that concentrated power, especially power unmoored from electoral accountability, tends toward tyranny. James Madison warned in Federalist No. 47 that "the accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny." Yet that is precisely what modern regulatory agencies represent: executive bodies that legislate, adjudicate, and enforce, combining all three constitutional powers in a single entity. The administrative state, as scholars have termed it, represents a constitutional revolution that the American people never consented to through the procedures the Constitution prescribes for amendment.

The solution is not to reform these agencies or make them more responsive, but to return the legislative power to Congress where it belongs. If Americans want environmental protections, Congress should pass environmental laws. If they want safer workplaces, their elected representatives should enact workplace safety legislation. This would restore democratic accountability—voters could hold their representatives responsible for the rules they create—and ensure that regulations receive the public scrutiny that constitutional lawmaking demands.

The Economic Case Against Regulation

Beyond constitutional concerns, federal regulatory agencies impose enormous economic costs that harm workers, consumers, and the broader prosperity of the nation. These costs take multiple forms, but all ultimately reduce the wealth and opportunity available to ordinary Americans.

The most immediate cost is compliance. When a company must navigate thousands of pages of EPA regulations, FDA approval processes, or SEC reporting requirements, it must hire lawyers, consultants, and compliance officers whose sole purpose is satisfying bureaucratic demands rather than creating value. These resources represent pure waste—effort that produces nothing useful for consumers but merely satisfies regulatory requirements. Studies have estimated that federal regulation costs the American economy over $2 trillion annually, a staggering sum that represents foregone investment, lower wages, and higher prices.

These compliance costs fall disproportionately on small businesses and new entrants, which lack the resources to navigate complex regulatory regimes. A startup with a promising new pharmaceutical compound may lack the millions of dollars needed to navigate FDA approval, condemning patients to inferior treatments and eliminating potential competition for established firms. Similarly, a small manufacturer may find OSHA compliance costs prohibitive, preventing it from entering markets and offering jobs to workers who need them. The result is economic concentration—larger firms that can afford compliance costs gain advantages over smaller competitors, reducing competition and its attendant benefits of lower prices, higher quality, and greater innovation.

Regulatory agencies also stifle innovation by creating uncertainty and delaying the introduction of new products. Consider the case of drug approval: the average new pharmaceutical takes over a decade and billions of dollars to bring to market, with much of that time and money devoted to satisfying FDA requirements rather than demonstrating safety and efficacy. During this delay, patients with serious conditions suffer and die awaiting treatments that exist but cannot reach them. The EPA's ever-shifting regulatory landscape discourages companies from investing in new technologies, as yesterday's compliant product may become tomorrow's violation. This dynamic is particularly harmful in environmental protection, where the most promising solutions often require novel approaches that existing regulations may not anticipate.

The Myth of Regulatory Competence

Supporters of federal regulatory agencies often assume that expert bureaucrats can identify and prevent harms more effectively than market forces or private legal action. This assumption, however, contradicts both theoretical reasoning and historical experience. Regulatory agencies suffer from inherent limitations that make them poor substitutes for decentralized market mechanisms and tort law.

First, regulators face a knowledge problem of almost insurmountable magnitude. The EPA employs thousands of scientists, yet they cannot possibly possess the specialized knowledge required to evaluate every chemical, manufacturing process, and environmental interaction under their purview. The FDA cannot realistically assess the safety and efficacy of every new drug with the thoroughness that proper medical evaluation requires. In contrast, markets harness the dispersed knowledge of millions of participants—scientists, investors, consumers, workers—who have strong incentives to identify both opportunities and dangers. When a product is unsafe, word gets around quickly in a free market; information flows far more rapidly through reputation, reviews, and social networks than through regulatory approval processes.

Second, regulatory agencies are captured by the industries they regulate. The phenomenon of regulatory capture, identified by economist George Stigler, describes how industries inevitably come to control the agencies tasked with overseeing them. Agency personnel seek employment in the industries they regulate, creating a revolving door that undermines independence. Industries provide the technical expertise that agencies require, enabling them to shape regulatory outcomes in their favor. The result is often regulation that benefits established firms by raising barriers to competition rather than protecting the public. Financial regulation, for example, often serves to advantage large financial institutions that can absorb compliance costs over smaller competitors, reducing competition and potentially increasing systemic risk.

Third, regulatory agencies face perverse incentives that make them either too permissive or overly restrictive in precisely the wrong circumstances. Agencies want to avoid scandals, so they tend to approve products quickly to avoid accusations of blocking beneficial innovations. But when disasters occur—as they occasionally will despite any regulatory system—agencies face intense political pressure to be seen doing something, often leading to overreaction and counterproductive restrictions. The tort system, by contrast, gets the incentives right: plaintiffs who are harmed can seek compensation, while firms that produce safe products face no liability. This creates appropriate incentives for care without the distortions inherent in regulatory decision-making.

The Private Law Alternative

If federal regulatory agencies are incompetent, unconstitutional, and economically harmful, what should replace them? The answer lies in private law—the system of torts, contracts, and property rights that has evolved over centuries to resolve disputes and protect rights without government supervision. Private legal action, combined with the discipline of market competition, can adequately address most of the concerns that regulatory agencies claim to handle.

Consider product safety. Under tort law, manufacturers who produce defective products that harm consumers face liability for the damages they cause. This creates powerful incentives for safety: every potential injury represents a potential lawsuit with substantial financial consequences. Firms have strong incentives to test products thoroughly, warn of dangers, and design safety into their products from the beginning. The tort system also has advantages over regulatory approval processes. It can respond quickly to new dangers as they emerge, without the delays inherent in rulemaking. It can calibrate liability to actual harm, rather than imposing one-size-fits-all requirements that may be excessive for some products and inadequate for others.

The objection that tort law provides inadequate deterrence because some defendants cannot pay or because litigation costs consume too much of the recovery has force, but it does not justify regulation. Better solutions include malpractice courts for specific industries, which can streamline litigation and reduce costs, or mandatory insurance requirements that ensure defendants can satisfy judgments. The proper response to imperfections in private law is to improve private law, not to replace it with a system that is even more flawed.

Environmental protection offers perhaps the strongest case for the private law alternative. Pollution harms people and property, and common-law nuisance doctrines have long provided remedies for such harms. If a factory's emissions damage a neighbor's crops or a neighbor's health, the affected party can sue for damages or seek an injunction. The challenge with environmental harms is often that they are diffuse—many polluters each contributing a small amount to a general problem, or many victims each suffering轻微 harm that does not justify individual litigation. This is where private property rights combined with class actions and associational standing can help: groups of affected parties can sue collectively, and the prospect of substantial liability for major polluters creates powerful incentives for environmental care.

Moreover, markets provide environmental protection through reputation and consumer choice. Consumers increasingly prefer environmentally responsible products, and firms respond to these preferences. The market for organic food, renewable energy, and sustainable products demonstrates that private actors can drive environmental improvement without government mandates. Investors increasingly recognize environmental risks, incorporating them into investment decisions and pressuring companies to improve their practices. This market-based environmentalism has achieved significant progress and promises more as public awareness grows.

Addressing the Collective Action Objection

The strongest objection to relying on private law and markets is that some problems involve collective action difficulties that individual lawsuits cannot address. Climate change is the paradigmatic example: no single polluter causes obvious harm to identifiable victims that a court could remedy. In such cases, the argument goes, government regulation is necessary to address harms that private law cannot reach.

This objection has merit, but it does not justify the existing regulatory state. First, the collective action problem is often overstated. Climate change involves many identifiable actors—major corporations whose emissions can be traced and whose products can be connected to specific harms. Tort theories are evolving to address such diffuse harms, and there is no reason to believe they cannot eventually provide remedies. The proper response to novel legal challenges is to develop the law, not to abandon it for bureaucratic decree.

Second, even where collective action problems genuinely exist, the appropriate response is targeted legislation authorizing specific remedies, not a permanent bureaucracy with sweeping powers. If climate change requires government action, Congress should enact a law that addresses it—imposing a carbon tax, say, or establishing a system of emissions trading. Such legislation would be subject to democratic debate and amendment, and its scope and duration could be calibrated to the problem. It would not create a permanent agency with power to regulate every aspect of energy production and consumption.

Third, we should be honest about what we do not know. The case for government intervention in collective action problems often assumes that government knows what policies will effectively address the problem and will implement them competently. History provides little basis for confidence in either assumption. Government programs frequently fail, and when they do, they impose costs that private action would not. The uncertainty surrounding complex problems like climate change suggests humility about our ability to design effective solutions through central planning.

The Moral Case for Freedom

Beyond practical and economic arguments, there is a moral case for abolishing regulatory agencies that transcends considerations of efficiency. Freedom is not merely a means to prosperity; it is a fundamental value that Americans have long cherished. The regulatory state undermines this freedom in ways that should disturb anyone who values human dignity and self-determination.

When the FDA delays approval of a promising cancer drug, it is not merely imposing economic costs; it is denying patients the opportunity to make their own choices about risk and hope. When the EPA restricts land use, it is not merely managing environmental risks; it is telling property owners what they may do with their own assets. When OSHA mandates workplace procedures, it is not merely ensuring safety; it is denying workers and employers the freedom to negotiate the terms of their cooperation. In each case, unelected bureaucrats are substituting their judgment for that of free individuals who are perfectly capable of making their own decisions.

This paternalism is particularly objectionable because it treats ordinary Americans as incapable of protecting themselves. The implicit premise of the regulatory state is that citizens need government guardians to shield them from dangerous products, harmful employment, and environmental degradation. But Americans are not children. They can read warnings, evaluate risks, and make choices that reflect their own values and circumstances. Some people choose to eat unhealthy food, work dangerous jobs, or live in polluted areas—and they have every right to do so. The proper role of government is to ensure that people have accurate information about risks and remedies for harms they suffer, not to substitute bureaucratic judgment for individual choice.

Reclaiming American Prosperity

The United States was built on a foundation of economic freedom, and its great prosperity flowed from that freedom. The eras of greatest growth and opportunity—the nineteenth century, the post-World War II boom, the Reagan and Clinton eras of deregulation—correlate strongly with reduced government intervention in the economy. By contrast, the regulatory expansion of the Progressive era, the New Deal, and the 1970s coincided with slower growth, higher unemployment, and diminished dynamism.

Abolishing federal regulatory agencies would not mean chaos or danger. It would mean returning to a system in which innovation flourishes, competition drives improvement, and individuals bear responsibility for their choices. Private law would provide remedies for genuine harms. Markets would discipline reckless behavior through reputation and the profit motive. And freedom—the freedom that makes America exceptional—would be restored.

The path forward requires neither moderate reform nor gradual adjustment. The regulatory state has grown so vast, so entrenched, and so damaging that only its complete abolition will suffice. Congress should repeal the laws that created these agencies and return their functions to the private sector and the states. The constitutional separation of powers should be restored. And the American people should once again be free to innovate, trade, and live as they see fit.

This is a radical agenda, but it is grounded in first principles and supported by evidence. The regulatory state has failed to deliver on its promises while imposing enormous costs. It is time to try freedom.

Economic Liberty and the Critique of Regulatory Intervention

The Principle of Voluntary Association

At its core, the argument for eliminating regulatory agencies begins with the principle that competent adults should have the liberty to make their own choices about risks, consumption, and employment without paternalistic interference from distant bureaucracies. This perspective holds that individuals possess sovereign authority over their own bodies, property, and labor, and that voluntary transactions between consenting parties require no governmental approval or oversight.

From this viewpoint, the very existence of regulatory agencies represents a fundamental violation of economic liberty. When the FDA prevents a terminally ill patient from accessing experimental treatments, or when OSHA prevents a worker from accepting a dangerous but well-compensated job, the government is substituting its judgment for that of competent individuals who are capable of making their own decisions. Advocates argue that this paternalism is both morally condescending and practically harmful, as it prevents the formation of valuable information through market processes.

Market Failures and Their Alternatives

Proponents of deregulation challenge the conventional understanding of market failures that justifies regulatory intervention. While economists traditionally point to externalities, information asymmetries, and public goods as justifications for government action, free-market advocates argue that clearly defined and enforced property rights can internalize externalities, that market mechanisms can solve information problems, and that private provision of public goods is both possible and often superior.

Consider environmental protection: rather than command-and-control regulations from the EPA, this perspective argues that robust property rights in air and water, combined with the ability to sue for damages, would create powerful incentives for pollution prevention. A factory that contaminates a neighbor's property would face liability costs that incentivize cleanup and prevention, while market mechanisms such as pollution permits could emerge organically to address residual harms. The regulatory approach, by contrast, creates political opportunities for special interests, generates compliance industries that consume resources without producing value, and often concentrates pollution in areas where regulatory enforcement is weakest.

Replacing Regulation with Private Ordering

Contract and Tort Remedies

The central alternative to federal regulation proposed by advocates is the existing system of common law torts and contractual remedies. Under this framework, individuals and businesses who are harmed by dangerous products, environmental contamination, unsafe working conditions, or fraudulent securities could seek redress through private lawsuits. The threat of liability, proponents argue, creates powerful incentives for safety and compliance that are more targeted and immediate than regulatory mandates.

This system has several claimed advantages over administrative regulation. First, liability costs are proportional to actual harms, whereas regulatory compliance often requires expenditures regardless of actual risk. Second, lawsuit incentives focus attention on genuine problems rather than bureaucratic priorities. Third, the adversarial process tests evidence and assigns responsibility in ways that administrative rulemaking does not. Fourth, damages awards compensate victims rather than funding bureaucratic overhead.

For workplace safety, advocates argue that the threat of wrongful death and injury lawsuits would compel employers to maintain safe conditions, particularly in dangerous industries where workers' compensation alone provides insufficient deterrence. Similarly, in securities markets, the threat of securities fraud litigation—potentially enhanced by class action mechanisms and contingency fees—would discipline bad actors more effectively than SEC enforcement, which proponents view as sporadic, politically influenced, and divorced from actual investor losses.

Reputation and Market Discipline

Beyond legal remedies, free-market advocates emphasize the role of reputation and market discipline in constraining harmful behavior. Companies that produce unsafe products, pollute excessively, or engage in fraud face reputational costs that translate into lost customers, higher insurance costs, and difficulty attracting talent. These market consequences often precede and exceed legal penalties, providing ongoing incentives for responsible behavior.

The rise of third-party certification, consumer advocacy organizations, and specialized media demonstrates that private information mechanisms can develop to fill gaps left by deregulation. Under this framework, consumers concerned about environmental practices could rely on eco-certification organizations; investors worried about fraud could subscribe to independent research services; workers concerned about safety could consult industry-specific publications and worker advocacy groups. These private alternatives, advocates argue, are more responsive to consumer preferences than one-size-fits-all regulatory mandates.

Agency-Specific Arguments

The Environmental Protection Agency

Critics of the EPA argue that environmental regulation should be handled through property rights enforcement and tort law rather than administrative mandates. The fundamental critique holds that the EPA's command-and-control approach sets arbitrary standards, creates massive compliance costs, and often achieves environmental improvements at unnecessarily high expense. The regulatory alternative, they argue, substitutes bureaucratic judgment for informed consumer and worker choice while creating compliance costs that are passed on to the same individuals regulation claims to protect.

The case for eliminating federal regulatory agencies rests on a vision of society where competent individuals make their own choices, where private ordering and market discipline constrain harmful behavior, and where legal remedies provide accountability for genuine harms. The deepest superstition of modern American politics is the belief that safety flows from Washington. We assume that without the Food and Drug Administration, poisoned pills would flood pharmacy shelves; that without the Environmental Protection Agency, rivers would burn; that without the Securities and Exchange Commission, every investor would be fleeced; that without the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, factories would become charnel houses. The EPA, FDA, OSHA, SEC, and their siblings should be abolished, and the work of protecting people returned to the institutions that actually perform it: competitive markets and enforceable legal rights.

Begin with the theory of regulation itself, which imagines disinterested experts pursuing the public interest. The reality, as Nobel laureate George Stigler demonstrated, is that agencies are political bodies staffed by people with careers, budgets, and ambitions—and they are reliably captured by the industries they oversee. The FDA's drug-review divisions are now funded substantially by fees from pharmaceutical companies, making the industry the agency's paying customer. SEC lawyers rotate seamlessly into Wall Street compliance departments. EPA rules are negotiated around incumbent technologies, freezing out the upstarts who might displace today's polluters with something cleaner. Even capture aside, regulators face Hayek's knowledge problem: no central bureau can aggregate the dispersed, tacit knowledge of millions of producers and consumers. Worse, agency incentives are grotesquely asymmetric. The FDA commissioner who approves a drug that later harms someone faces congressional hearings and ruin; the commissioner who delays a life-saving therapy for a decade is invisible, because the victims of delay never make the news. The result is a system biased toward suffocating caution, with costs that fall on people who never learn what was withheld from them.

Consider the record. After the 1962 amendments empowered the FDA to demand proof of efficacy, economist Sam Peltzman found that new drug introductions collapsed, development costs soared, and measurable safety gains were essentially nil. Americans have since endured a chronic "drug lag," waiting years for therapies already available in Europe—beta-blockers among them—with researchers estimating the death toll of delay in the tens of thousands. This is the FDA's "invisible graveyard," and the agency effectively confessed to it when Congress passed Right to Try in 2018, admitting that terminal patients deserved to bypass the FDA entirely. During the early COVID-19 outbreak, FDA and CDC restrictions blocked private and academic labs from deploying tests for crucial weeks. Nor does approval guarantee safety: Vioxx and fen-phen were duly approved before being withdrawn amid tens of thousands of estimated injuries—and thanks to doctrines like the preemption recognized in Riegel v. Medtronic, FDA approval can strip injured patients of their right to sue. Even the FDA's finest hour, the thalidomide decision, was the act of a single cautious reviewer—a function that private certifiers, physicians, pharmacists, and liability exposure all perform. The United States Pharmacopeia, a private body, was standardizing drug quality eighty-six years before the FDA existed.

The SEC's record is, if anything, more damning. Harry Markopolos handed the agency Bernie Madoff's fraud on a platter—repeatedly, over nearly a decade—and was brushed off while the agency busied itself with paperwork violations. Sarbanes-Oxley imposed billions in compliance costs that fall hardest on small firms, throttled the small-company IPO market, and entrenched the very incumbents whose frauds inspired it. Accredited-investor rules decree that ordinary Americans may buy lottery tickets but not startup equity. The SEC's own creation of the NRSRO designation handed Moody's, S&P, and Fitch a government-granted oligopoly whose rubber stamps anesthetized investors before 2008. And who actually exposed the great frauds of our era? Jim Chanos and other short sellers flagged Enron. Hindenburg Research exposed Nikola, whose founder was then convicted in court by ordinary fraud prosecutors—tools that would survive the SEC's abolition intact. Markets and criminal law caught the crooks; the regulator wrote rules.

OSHA and the EPA fare no better under scrutiny. The workplace fatality rate fell by more than half in the four decades before OSHA was created in 1970, driven by rising wealth, better technology, and the wage premiums that dangerous jobs must pay to attract workers; economists studying OSHA's marginal impact have found it surprisingly small relative to that preexisting trend, while its output in paperwork and technology-freezing standards is immense. The EPA's Superfund program has consumed tens of billions of dollars over four decades, much of it devoured by litigation among potentially responsible parties, while designated sites languish. The Clean Air Act's New Source Review perversely grandfathered the dirtiest old coal plants, rewarding utilities for keeping them running. And urban air was already improving before 1970—Pittsburgh's smoke ordinances and the switch from coal to natural gas did their work in the 1940s and 1950s—because environmental quality is a normal good that wealth purchases, and wealth is generated by markets. It is no accident that the economically freest nations consistently top global environmental performance rankings.

Underwriters Laboratories, founded in 1894, tests products by the billion; its mark is demanded by insurers, retailers, and consumers. The National Fire Protection Association, a private nonprofit, writes the electrical code that municipalities adopt. Private kosher and organic certification agencies police the food supply for millions of Americans with a rigor no bureaucracy matches, sustained purely by the value of their credibility. Tort law would punish and deter, as it did when asbestos litigation accomplished what decades of regulation never did: it bankrupted an entire industry and removed a deadly product from commerce. The choice was never between regulation and nothing. It is between two systems for discovering truth and punishing harm: monopoly bureaucracies with perverse incentives, captured by their charges, blind to dispersed knowledge, and accountable to no victim—or the distributed intelligence of competitive markets disciplined by enforceable rights, where every seller's fortune depends on not poisoning, maiming, or defrauding the customer. The agencies had their century, their budgets, and their vast authority, and the result is delay, capture, unseen casualties, and two trillion dollars a year in dead weight on the freedom that made Americans safe and prosperous in the first place. Abolish the agencies. Keep the courts. Trust free people, liable for the harm they cause, to do what they have always done better than their overseers.

Abolish the Federal Regulatory State

The Environmental Protection Agency, Food and Drug Administration, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, Securities and Exchange Commission, and similar federal bodies are commonly portrayed as indispensable guardians of public welfare. Yet these agencies often impose enormous costs, suppress competition, delay innovation, and separate decision-making from accountability. Safety, honesty, and environmental stewardship are legitimate goals, but centralized federal bureaucracy is neither the only nor the best way to achieve them. Congress should abolish the major federal regulatory agencies and replace their command-and-control systems with enforceable property rights, private certification, competitive insurance, state and local governance, and direct legal remedies for people who suffer harm.

Federal regulation restricts economic freedom by replacing voluntary choices with uniform rules written by distant officials. Agencies routinely dictate which products may be sold, how workplaces must operate, what risks consumers may accept, and which technologies may enter the market. Even when rules are well intentioned, they cannot account for every difference among industries, communities, workers, and consumers. A standard that is manageable for a multinational corporation may be ruinous for a small business. A drug-approval requirement intended to prevent unsafe products may also delay treatments for patients willing to accept greater risk. A workplace rule designed for a factory may make little sense for a family-owned workshop.

Such regulation also tends to favor established firms. Large corporations can maintain compliance departments, hire specialized lawyers, lobby agencies, and absorb years of administrative delay. Startups and small businesses cannot. The result is regulatory capture: agencies that supposedly restrain concentrated economic power often help preserve it by raising barriers to entry. Regulation therefore does not simply limit markets; it can insulate dominant businesses from market competition.

The better alternative is to make those who cause harm directly accountable. If a company poisons a river, injures workers through negligence, sells a dangerously defective product, or defrauds investors, the victims should be able to recover full damages through the courts. Injunctions should stop ongoing harm, punitive damages should address reckless misconduct, and losing defendants should bear appropriate legal costs. Clear property rights and accessible courts would focus enforcement on actual injury rather than on technical violations that may have caused no harm at all.

Private institutions would reinforce this legal accountability. Insurers already have strong incentives to inspect workplaces, evaluate products, and demand risk-reducing practices from policyholders. Independent laboratories and certification organizations can test food, medicine, machinery, and consumer goods. Stock exchanges, auditors, lenders, and rating agencies can impose disclosure and governance requirements on companies seeking access to capital. Consumers, employees, investors, and local communities can choose among competing standards instead of being trapped under a single federal regime.

Unlike government agencies, private certifiers must protect their reputations. A certification body that repeatedly approves dangerous products loses customers and faces liability. A federal agency that makes serious mistakes usually receives another appropriation, additional authority, and promises of internal reform. Competition permits failed institutions to be replaced; bureaucracy protects them from replacement.

The FDA illustrates the hidden costs of precautionary regulation. When an unsafe treatment is approved, the victims are visible. When a beneficial treatment is delayed or rejected, those harmed are dispersed and often invisible. Patients may die waiting, firms may abandon promising research, and innovators may avoid fields where approval is especially costly. A competitive system of private testing and certification would allow patients and physicians to choose different levels of evidentiary assurance while preserving strong remedies against fraud and concealed risks.

The same logic applies to environmental protection. Pollution is not a failure of freedom but an invasion of other people’s property and health. The answer should be to identify polluters, establish causation, stop the harmful activity, and require compensation—not to grant a federal agency broad power to micromanage vast sectors of the economy. Local communities also possess knowledge that national regulators lack. Environmental priorities in an industrial harbor, farming region, dense city, and remote wilderness need not be identical. Courts, states, municipalities, landowners, conservation organizations, and market-based systems can respond more flexibly than a uniform federal bureaucracy.

OSHA likewise substitutes detailed national rules for the incentives created by liability, insurance, reputation, and worker choice. These mechanisms target genuine risk while allowing different industries to develop practices suited to their circumstances.

The SEC’s stated mission can also be pursued through ordinary laws against fraud, contractual disclosure requirements, exchange rules, audits, and private litigation. Investors do not need Washington to guarantee that every investment is wise; they need reliable information and effective remedies when they are deliberately deceived. Competitive exchanges could require stricter disclosure from firms seeking their listings, while investors willing to bear more risk could choose less restrictive markets.

Abolition should not mean an overnight legal vacuum. Congress should repeal agency mandates in stages, transfer pending claims to courts, preserve laws against fraud, negligence, trespass, and pollution, and strengthen the ability of injured parties to obtain evidence and meaningful compensation. Government could continue operating courts and enforcing judgments without maintaining vast administrative systems that combine legislative, executive, and quasi-judicial authority.

No system eliminates risk or misconduct. Federal agencies certainly do not. Their failures are simply obscured by official authority and spread across the public. A free society should judge institutions not by their declared intentions but by their incentives, accountability, and results. Private certification and insurance can adapt rapidly to new evidence. Federal bureaucracies, by contrast, centralize mistakes, entrench incumbents, and restrict peaceful choices.

Safety and freedom are not opposites. Properly understood, both depend on responsibility: the freedom to innovate and exchange, paired with strict accountability for fraud, negligence, and coercive harm. Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for eliminating all federal regulatory agencies like the EPA, FDA, OSHA, and SEC, focusing on how this would promote economic liberty and rely on market forces and private lawsuits instead of government intervention.
Model Response:

Advocates of eliminating federal regulatory agencies such as the EPA, FDA, OSHA, and SEC generally make a libertarian or classical-liberal case: individuals and firms should be free to make voluntary arrangements, while courts—not administrative bureaucracies—should address actual harm. Their main arguments are:

Claimed benefits

  • Greater economic liberty: Businesses and workers could choose their own products, contracts, workplace practices, and levels of risk without needing federal permission.
  • Lower compliance costs: Eliminating licensing, reporting, testing, and procedural requirements could reduce legal and administrative expenses, especially for small firms.
  • More competition and innovation: Proponents argue that complex rules often protect established companies that can afford compliance, while deterring startups and slowing new drugs, technologies, and business models.
  • Lower prices and faster growth: Reduced compliance costs might translate into cheaper goods, increased investment, more hiring, and quicker introduction of products.
  • Less regulatory capture: Agencies can be influenced by the industries they regulate. Abolitionists contend that removing agencies would also remove a mechanism through which incumbent firms shape rules to disadvantage competitors.
  • Clearer political accountability: Congress would have to legislate directly rather than delegate broad authority to unelected officials, and courts would resolve disputes under ordinary law.
  • Fewer uniform federal mandates: States, insurers, certification organizations, industries, and consumers could adopt different standards suited to local conditions and preferences.

How market-based regulation is supposed to work

Under this view, regulation would not disappear entirely; it would shift to decentralized mechanisms:

  • Consumer choice and reputation: Unsafe or dishonest firms would lose customers after poor reviews, investigative reporting, product comparisons, or public disclosure.
  • Private certification: Organizations analogous to Underwriters Laboratories, accounting auditors, professional associations, and environmental certifiers could verify safety or quality.
  • Insurance requirements: Insurers could demand inspections, safety systems, audits, or environmental precautions before issuing coverage.
  • Contracts and supply chains: Buyers, lenders, exchanges, and large retailers could require quality, labor, disclosure, or environmental standards from counterparties.
  • Competition among states: States could maintain their own rules, allowing residents and businesses to compare regulatory systems.
  • Private lawsuits: People injured by pollution, defective products, dangerous workplaces, fraud, or securities misconduct could sue for damages or injunctions under tort, contract, property, and fraud law. Large damage awards would theoretically deter misconduct.

For example, supporters might replace FDA premarket approval with manufacturer liability and private certification; OSHA rules with insurance inspections and employee lawsuits; EPA controls with property-rights and nuisance suits; and SEC disclosure mandates with exchange rules, audits, contractual disclosure, and fraud litigation.

The underlying philosophical reasons

The case rests on several beliefs:

  1. Government should punish demonstrated harm rather than prohibit conduct in advance.
  2. Individuals are generally better judges of acceptable risk than federal officials.
  3. Prices, competition, reputation, insurance, and liability transmit information more effectively than centralized rulemaking.
  4. Administrative agencies combine legislative, executive, and adjudicative powers in ways critics consider insufficiently accountable.
  5. Regulation often produces unseen costs—lost products, jobs, investments, and innovations—that may exceed its visible benefits.

Major objections

Critics argue that markets and lawsuits frequently act after serious or irreversible harm has occurred and may fail where there are:

  • pollution and other harms imposed on third parties;
  • consumers who cannot evaluate drug, food, workplace, or financial risks;
  • long delays between conduct and injury;
  • insolvent defendants or damages exceeding a firm’s assets;
  • expensive litigation and difficulty proving causation;
  • dispersed victims with individually small claims;
  • monopoly power, secrecy, or weak competition;
  • workers unable to bargain effectively over safety;
  • systemic risks, such as financial contagion.

Private certification can also suffer conflicts of interest, and reputation works poorly when misconduct is hidden. Consequently, even many advocates of deregulation favor reform, simplification, stronger cost-benefit review, or transferring authority to states rather than abolishing every federal regulator. The core dispute is whether preventive public rules or decentralized market and legal remedies handle these failures more effectively—and at lower cost.

Prompt:

Model Response:

Abolishing major federal regulatory agencies such as the EPA, FDA, OSHA, and SEC would be a decisive step toward restoring economic freedom and accountability in American public life. These agencies were created to manage complex modern risks, but their real-world behavior has drifted toward a more fundamental problem: they replace individual choice and market discipline with centralized authority that is insulated from the very constraints that private actors face. The result is not merely inefficiency—it is systematic harm to liberty, prosperity, innovation, and ultimately the safety and fairness people claim to want. If we trust free markets and enforceable private rights, we can secure safety, environmental protection, and market integrity without empowering bureaucratic rule-making that exceeds democratic and economic limits.

1. Regulation substitutes bureaucratic power for consumer and worker choice

The core justification for abolishing federal regulatory agencies is simple: in a free society, individuals and voluntary institutions should be the primary drivers of economic decisions. Federal regulators are not elected by the people they affect, yet they wield authority to restrict products, shut down workplaces, and limit investment and speech. That means economic outcomes are increasingly determined by compliance strategies designed for bureaucratic preferences rather than by consumer demand, contract, and competition.

When agencies restrict economic activity through licensing, standards, enforcement actions, and discretionary interpretations, firms respond less by innovating to meet customer needs and more by lobbying, hiring compliance bureaucrats, and shaping internal processes to anticipate regulatory scrutiny. Those incentives distort markets. Resources flow into paperwork and political influence instead of research, productivity, and quality. Even when regulation is motivated by good intentions, the mechanism undermines economic freedom.

Abolishing agencies would re-center decision-making where it belongs: in the private sphere—between buyers and sellers, workers and employers, and investors and companies—under the discipline of enforceable contracts, tort law, and competitive pressure.

2. Free markets already create incentives for safety and quality—laws ensure accountability

Critics often claim that without regulators, markets will fail to protect people from dangerous products, workplace hazards, fraud, or environmental harm. But that argument overlooks how private legal systems function in a society that takes rights seriously.

Safety and quality through liability

If a consumer is harmed by a defective medical device, unsafe drug, contaminated food, or fraudulent advertisement, existing legal doctrines—product liability, negligence, breach of warranty, and consumer protection law—provide remedies. These remedies are not symbolic. They can include compensation, injunctions, punitive damages in appropriate cases, and legal costs that deter wrongdoing. The prospect of being sued directly impacts business behavior. Firms have strong incentives to design safer products, maintain quality control, and truthfully disclose risks because the market can punish them only when harmed parties can recover.

Workplace safety through tort and wage bargaining

Workplace hazards can also be addressed without OSHA-like centralized mandates. Workers can sue employers for negligence and unsafe conditions. Insurance markets price risk, and employers have incentives to reduce accidents to lower claims and premiums. In many settings, labor markets and unions (where present) negotiate safety standards contractually. Free entry, reputation, and competitive contracting all pressure employers to avoid preventable injuries.

Abolishing OSHA does not mean abandoning worker protection; it means shifting from regulatory command-and-control to individualized accountability and market-driven risk management—supported by tort law and insurance.

Environmental harm through private and public nuisance, property rights, and cleanup liability

Environmental protection is often framed as a task requiring federal agencies, but environmental damage is, at its heart, a harm to persons and property. When a factory pollutes a river, it violates rights and imposes costs on downstream residents, businesses, and ecosystems. Private law already includes tools to address these harms: nuisance, trespass, negligence, property damage, and strict-liability doctrines in certain circumstances. In addition, businesses face market consequences—lost customers, reputational damage, and higher insurance and financing costs—when they pollute.

Moreover, environmental cleanup can be structured through litigation and enforceable settlements, as it already often is in the real world. If we made those private remedies faster, less procedurally clogged, and more reliable, the need for expansive federal rulemaking would diminish.

Financial markets through disclosure and fraud enforcement

The SEC’s core mission—securities fraud prevention and disclosure—can be handled largely through private lawsuits and existing common-law fraud and contract principles, combined with criminal enforcement by prosecutors for clear wrongdoing. Markets require credible information. Firms that mislead investors should face severe civil liability and, where appropriate, criminal penalties. Private class actions and arbitration regimes (where enforceable) provide incentives to uncover and litigate fraud. If disclosure rules were less prescriptive, companies would still have to be truthful to avoid liability, because investors can sue for deception and seek damages.

In other words: we do not need to choose between “no oversight” and “centralized bureaucratic rule-making.” We can choose accountability built on enforceable rights and market discipline.

3. Agencies create regulatory capture and political entanglement

Even when regulation begins as a response to real risks, the institutional incentives of agencies encourage regulatory capture. Regulated industries and interest groups inevitably influence rule-writing, guidance interpretation, enforcement priorities, and compliance frameworks. Over time, agencies can become instruments of the very stakeholders they purport to police.

Capture is not an accident; it is an outcome of incentives:

  • Agencies require ongoing cooperation and information from firms.
  • Firms therefore gain influence over what regulators measure and how they interpret compliance.
  • Enforcement discretion creates opportunities for negotiation and selective pressure.
  • Compliance burdens become predictable costs that can be used to advantage incumbents over new entrants.

This dynamic harms economic freedom by entrenching established players and restricting innovation. It can also reduce safety in practice: if enforcement targets are skewed toward paperwork rather than actual risk, the system can incentivize form over substance.

Abolishing major federal agencies would disrupt these cycles and shift authority back to courts and consumers—institutions that must justify actions through transparent legal standards and adversarial proof.

4. Centralized regulation is slow, rigid, and out of touch with real risk

Technology and markets evolve quickly. Federal agencies often move slowly due to rulemaking processes, cost-benefit analysis frameworks, and litigation over agency interpretations. By the time rules take effect, the underlying risk landscape may have changed. The agency also must apply uniform standards across diverse regions, companies, and contexts, even though risks are not uniform.

Private legal action can adapt more rapidly. If a new product hazard emerges, affected individuals and businesses can file suit, and courts can interpret existing law—negligence, defectiveness, fraud, misrepresentation—based on the facts of the case. This case-by-case approach does not eliminate uncertainty, but it avoids the “one-size-fits-all” problem of administrative command.

Moreover, the private liability model naturally concentrates enforcement on concrete harm. Regulators, by contrast, can impose rules preemptively and expand compliance obligations even before harm occurs. That means agency power can outgrow actual evidence of benefit.

5. Regulatory agencies frequently produce unintended consequences that undermine the very goals they pursue

When government regulates to prevent harm, it can generate new ones:

  • Cost externalization: Compliance costs can lead firms to cut corners elsewhere or shift production to less regulated jurisdictions (including globally).
  • Barriers to entry: Complex regulatory frameworks can prevent startups and small businesses from competing, concentrating market power.
  • Incentives for “compliance theater”: If success is defined by meeting formal requirements rather than reducing real-world harm, companies may optimize documentation.
  • Innovation suppression: Product reformulation, delayed launch schedules, and legal uncertainty can reduce beneficial innovation.

Abolishing agencies forces a different system: firms must manage risks to avoid liability and to meet consumer preferences. That approach directly aligns incentives with outcomes rather than administrative paperwork.

6. Fairness and protection are better achieved through private rights, courts, and voluntary standards

Abolishing federal regulatory agencies might sound like abandoning safeguards, but a rights-based alternative can be more protective—because it is grounded in actual harms and enforced by parties with clear stakes.

To ensure safety and fairness in a truly market-based system, society can rely on:

  • Strong tort liability and product liability standards that reward safer design and truthful warnings.
  • Robust consumer protection and fraud enforcement through private litigation.
  • Insurance and risk-based contracting that price harm and incentivize prevention.
  • Common-law defenses and evidentiary rules that improve accuracy and reduce arbitrary outcomes.
  • Voluntary industry standards and professional licensing at state level, where they can be tailored locally and contested legally.

Courts can also serve as “feedback loops” for what the law should require as new technologies emerge. The adversarial system tests claims about harm and causation in a way that rulemaking cannot replicate.

Conclusion: Economic freedom and safety are allies, not enemies

The strongest argument for abolishing major federal regulatory agencies is that they undermine economic freedom while providing protections that can be achieved—often more effectively—through private rights and market discipline. Free markets do not mean chaos; they mean competition, choice, and accountability. When individuals and businesses can sue for concrete harms, when fraud and negligence carry real consequences, and when insurance and reputation reward prevention, safety, fairness, and environmental responsibility can be enforced without administrative overreach.

The question is not whether people deserve protection. They do. The question is who should be empowered to provide it. In a society committed to liberty and prosperity, protection should flow from enforceable private rights and transparent legal processes—not from unelected administrative institutions whose incentives favor compliance burdens, political influence, and rigidity. Abolishing these agencies would be a powerful step toward returning power to individuals, strengthening courts, and allowing markets to deliver both freedom and responsibility.
